JayatsenSharma

It began with a screen glowing in a small room, and a boy who wanted to know what lived inside it.

Engineering taught me how things are built. A curiosity about brands, and the quiet ideas behind every advertisement, taught me why they matter.

So I chose marketing, then carried it onto the shop floor, where every idea has to meet a customer and earn its sale.

Projects.

GCL

Global Citizen Leadership

IPSA · Nov '25–Mar '26

Team House Stark (Group 5) asked why so few women guard India's private spaces, then built a product to change it.

01The questionProblem
  • TOPICDiversity, equity and inclusion in India's male-dominated private security sector.
  • GAPA 14:1 male-to-female ratio.
  • BARRIERSSocial barriers, safety concerns around the job, and limited career growth.
02What we foundTwo surveys · 400 responses
  • GUARDS200 women guards: 52% had considered leaving because of society, and pay parity scored lowest (2.46 of 5).
  • CLIENTS200 clients and agencies: 54.5% want male guards only, 41.5% a mix. That appetite for mixed teams is the opening.

Women guards Agencies Clients

Pay is equal
28%46%41%
Training is equal
32%55%51%
Facilities are adequate
34%50%38%
Diversity is included
33%52%58%

Agencies and clients assume safety and fairness. The guards' own numbers say otherwise: a pay gap of about 18% and a training gap of about 20%.

03The solutionFive moves
  • ONE NAMEEveryone is a "Guard", with no gendered titles.
  • MIXED TEAMSWomen deployed in structured mixed teams, such as alternate floors or zones.
  • TRAININGRole clarity and situational handling over physical strength.
  • RATIOFrom 14:1 to 7.5:1 over two years, through pilots and phased scaling.
  • FEEDBACKA dual-feedback app: clients rate guards, women guards report conditions.
04VeeranganaThe app
  • MY PARTProduct strategy and UI/UX.
  • CLIENT SIDEEmployer portal with a deployment snapshot, floor coverage map, incident alerts and reports.
  • GUARD SIDEPerformance rating, shifts, FaceID check-in and an emergency flare; guards rate employers too.
  • REVENUEThe agency pays the platform per guard deployed.

Fields I know and follow

These are not roles or services. They are the areas I have learned on my own and keep up with.

Code

  • JavaOOP and design patterns, collections and generics, streams, multithreading, and how the JVM manages memory and garbage collection.
  • C++Pointers and references, RAII, STL containers and algorithms, templates, and manual memory management without leaks.
  • Core CSData structures, algorithms and Big-O analysis, plus OS, DBMS and networking fundamentals.
  • WebSemantic HTML, CSS Grid and Flexbox, responsive layout, vanilla JavaScript and the DOM, accessibility, and load performance.

PC hardware

  • CPUCores and threads, cache hierarchy, boost clocks, sockets and chipsets, and TDP versus real power draw.
  • GPUShader and CUDA cores, VRAM size and bus width, ray tracing, and upscaling with DLSS and FSR.
  • MemoryDDR4 versus DDR5, CAS latency and timings, dual-channel setups, and XMP and EXPO profiles.
  • StorageNVMe Gen 4 and Gen 5 versus SATA, TLC versus QLC, DRAM cache, and sustained write speeds.
  • Board and PSUVRM quality, PCIe lanes and chipset tiers; PSU wattage, 80 Plus ratings and the ATX 3.x connector.
  • CoolingAir versus AIO, thermal paste, case airflow and fan curves, and keeping thermals in check.
  • DisplaysPanel types (IPS, VA, OLED), refresh rate, response time and adaptive sync.
  • Build logicBalancing parts to avoid bottlenecks, price-to-performance, and planning upgrade paths.

Tech industry

  • SiliconIntel, AMD and Nvidia product cycles; TSMC and process nodes; x86 versus ARM and Apple silicon.
  • Memory marketWhy DRAM and NAND prices swing, and how that feeds into RAM and SSD pricing.
  • AI hardwareData-centre GPUs and accelerators, and why HBM and packaging capacity limit supply.
  • LaunchesReading a launch: benchmarks against marketing claims, pricing tiers, refreshes and positioning.
